newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gabon flies home Rwandan refugees and fugitives.
newsitem.headline: Gabon flies home Rwandan refugees and fugitives.

text.p: Gabon has sent home to Rwanda the last 168 refugees and fugitives who fled there last year, the United Nations refugee agency reported on Tuesday.

Spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole said the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees was trying to learn the fate of 123 Hutu men who were "handcuffed, put in military pickups and sent to an unknown destination" after landing in Kigali.

She also condemned Gabon for forcibly sending home eight Rwandans whom UNHCR had recognised as genuine refugees needing international protection. Gabon acted before the agency could finish its assessments to distinguish innocent refugees from fugitive participants in Rwanda's 1994 genocide.

Among those sent home on military planes overnight were 43 soldiers of the former Rwandan government army and some civilians who had admitted having taken part in an attempted hijacking during an aborted attempt to send them home from Gabon last Saturday, she told a news briefing.
Some 45 women and children who landed on Tuesday are to be registered before being moved to their communes, O'Toole said.
"We strongly condemn the forcible repatriation of the eight refugees of concern to UNHCR. It is a flagrant violation of basic human rights and humanitarian principles," she said.
"We want access to these people. It is vital to talk at least to the eight refugees recognised as such whom we were led to believe would be allowed to stay for some time".
The overnight repatriation, in two Antonov military aircraft, means all 1,100 displaced Rwandans who trekked to Gabon this year have returned to their homeland, according to UNHCR.

Gabon is 1,600 km (1,000 miles) west of Rwanda. The Rwandans, who had earlier sought safety in Zaire, fled to and across Congo-Libreville to escape the war which turned Zaire into the Democratic Republic of the Congo
The Rwandans, who were being screened by UNHCR to determine their status in recent weeks, included about 100 whom the Gabonese government said had volunteered to go home.

Last Friday, UNHCR announced it had begun cooperating with a U.N. war crimes tribunal hunting ringleaders of Rwanda's 1994 genocide. The agency said it was assisting investigators from the Arusha-based tribunal investigating the Hutu-led slaughter of more than half a million minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

A large proportion of those who reached Gabon were soldiers of the former Rwandan army, which played a key role in the genocide, and included high-ranking ex-officers. A Tutsi-dominated government took power in Kigali after the Hutu administration collapsed.
UNHCR had only managed to screen 26 ex-soldiers and 17 civilians before the first botched repatriation attempt.
Sadako Ogata, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, had personally asked Gabonese authorities to allow the screening to be completed before anyone was sent back, O'Toole said.

"Unless we were allowed to carry out screening, we cannot say with certainty who among them might have been involved in the genocide, or if any of them might have a claim to international protection," she added.
